title: Corey's prostaglandin F₂α (1969)
goal: Five stereocentres on a cyclopentane, set by a bicycle: how Corey made prostaglandin F₂α from cyclopentadiene.

problemSets.title: Building the lactone
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A Diels–Alder reaction with a ketene equivalent, then a Baeyer–Villiger, turn cyclopentadiene into a bicyclic lactone.
problemSets.conceptCard:
The **prostaglandins** are hormone-like fatty acids made in almost every tissue. PGF₂α has a cyclopentane carrying **four substituents on adjacent carbons**, two side chains and two OH groups, with five stereocentres in all. In 1969 E. J. Corey made it by a route still taught as a model of *stereocontrol*: build a rigid **bicycle**, where the shape decides which face reacts, then cut it open.

- **Diels–Alder**: 5-(methoxymethyl)cyclopentadiene and 2-chloroacrylonitrile give a bicyclo[2.2.1]heptene. The dienophile adds to the face away from the CH₂OMe group.
- **Ketene equivalent**: ketene would give the ketone directly, but it does [2+2] reactions instead. The carbon carrying Cl and CN is converted into a C=O by hydroxide: the CN is a removable handle.
- **Baeyer–Villiger**: mCPBA inserts an oxygen next to the ketone. The more substituted bridgehead carbon migrates, with **retention of configuration**, so the bicycle becomes a lactone without losing any stereochemistry.

The unmasking route drawn here (hydroxide adds to the nitrile; a neighbouring O⁻ replaces the chloride; the cyanohydrin loses cyanide) is a reasonable model built from textbook steps; the detailed pathway in KOH/DMSO has not been settled by experiment.

The app does not check stereochemistry yet: the problems ask for the arrows, and the text explains the faces.

setItems.whyThisOne: Warm-up: the Baeyer–Villiger on cyclohexanone, without a bicycle.
One concerted step builds the bicycle and sets the first stereocentres.
Hydroxide turns C(Cl)CN into C=O: the ketene equivalent pays off.
Which carbon migrates? The bridgehead, with retention.

problemSets.title: Iodolactonisation
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Iodine and an internal carboxylate add anti across the ring C=C, then a tin radical chain removes the iodine.
problemSets.conceptCard:
Aqueous NaOH opens the bicyclic lactone to a **cyclopentene** carrying CH₂CO₂⁻, OH and CH₂OMe, all fixed on the faces set by the bicycle. Two stereocentres are still missing.

**Iodolactonisation** (I₂ in aqueous KI, NaHCO₃):

- the C=C attacks iodine; an **iodonium ion** forms on the face away from the carboxylate
- the carboxylate opens it from the **opposite face** (anti addition), closing a **five-membered lactone**
- the result is a cis-fused γ-lactone: the oxygen that will become a ring OH of the prostaglandin is now on the right face

The iodine was only a handle. After protecting the free OH as an acetate, Corey removed it with **tributyltin hydride** and a little **AIBN**: a radical chain in which Bu₃Sn• takes the iodine atom and the carbon radical takes a hydrogen atom from Bu₃SnH. Half-arrows (fish-hooks) move one electron each.

Stereochemistry is explained here; the app does not check it yet.

setItems.whyThisOne: Warm-up: a bromonium ion opened anti by bromide.
The same anti addition, with the nucleophile built into the molecule.
A radical chain swaps iodine for hydrogen.

problemSets.title: Side chains
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons reaction adds the lower chain as an (E)-enone; a Wittig reaction adds the upper chain as a (Z)-alkene.
problemSets.conceptCard:
After deiodination, BBr₃ removed the methyl ether and Collins oxidation (CrO₃·pyridine, not drawn) gave **Corey's aldehyde**, an intermediate still made industrially for prostaglandin drugs. The two side chains are added with phosphorus reagents, and each gives a different alkene geometry.

- **Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons**: a phosphonate anion, stabilised by a ketone, adds reversibly to the aldehyde. The reaction passes through the less crowded oxaphosphetane and gives the **(E)-enone**. The by-product, a dimethyl phosphate salt, washes out with water.
- Between the two (not drawn): reduction of the enone ketone to the allylic alcohol, removal of the acetate, THP protection of both OH groups, and DIBAL reduction of the lactone to a **lactol**.
- **Wittig**: the lactol is a masked aldehyde. With base its ring opens, and an **unstabilised ylide** under salt-free conditions forms the oxaphosphetane fast and irreversibly with the two chains cis: the **(Z)-alkene** of the upper chain. Removing the THP groups gives PGF₂α.

Both reactions end the same way: a four-membered P–C–C–O ring falls apart to a C=C and a strong P=O.

setItems.whyThisOne: Warm-up: the plain Wittig reaction and its oxaphosphetane.
A stabilised phosphonate anion and an (E)-enone.
A masked aldehyde and an unstabilised ylide: the (Z)-alkene.

problemSets.title: Checkpoint
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Corey's synthesis, step by step, shuffled with the names hidden.
problemSets.conceptCard:
The reactions of this track in random order and without their names. For each one, ask:

- is it polar, pericyclic or radical: full arrows, a ring of arrows, or half-arrows?
- which group is the electrophile, and is there a more reactive one in the same molecule?
- for a ring closure or a rearrangement: which atoms end up bonded, and what size of ring forms?
- which face reacts, and why (told in the text: the app does not check it yet)?
